scripts.opening:opening:
[warmly] JAUNT: MONDAY AT THE FORTRESS. Monday morning, 21 November 1904, at the corner of Eighteenth Street and Prairie Avenue.

Five stops in and around the Glessner House. [short pause] Today is a Monday, which means the Reading Class: the wives of University of Chicago professors and the ladies of the South Side, gathering in the library at the invitation of Frances Glessner. [short pause] [amused] Inside these walls everything runs like a clock, and servants are rarely seen. [short pause] [softly] Across Eighteenth Street, in the house of the piano king, [sadly] the clock is running down.

[short pause] Start at the corner, where the neighbours first saw what Richardson had built.
scripts.stop:fortress: [measured] The corner of Eighteenth and Prairie. The house is granite, low and hard, with windows on the street side barely wide enough to light a corridor. Its architect, H. H. Richardson, died in 1886 before it was finished; it went up between June 1886 and December 1887. [short pause] [amused] Not everyone liked it. George Pullman, just across the way, complained: [grumbling] "I do not know what I have ever done to have that thing staring me in the face every time I go out of my door". [short pause] Pullman is seven years dead now, [chuckles] and the house is still staring. [short pause] [warmly] What the passers-by never see is the other side: generous windows onto a sunny courtyard, and a household that runs like a machine. [short pause] The ladies are arriving on foot.
scripts.stop:hostess: [warmly] The front door. In 1893 William Rainey Harper, the president of the new University of Chicago, asked Frances Glessner how the professors' wives might meet the women of the city. [short pause] Her answer was this: the Monday Morning Reading Class. It meets in the library for two hours every Monday from October to May. For the first hour the ladies sew while a professional reader reads aloud; the second hour is lighter, a reading or a lecture. [short pause] [amused] Nobody joins by asking. "Membership was by invitation only", and for a professor's wife new to Chicago an invitation is the way in. Mrs. Glessner greets her guests herself. Christine Nelson, the parlor maid, stands ready for their wraps. [short pause] [softly] Then the door shuts, and the house does what it was built to do.
scripts.stop:hall: [curious] Inside, the house turns its back on the street and opens to the courtyard. The door to the court has yellow glass under chipped white glass, which gives the hall "a feeling of sunlight even in cloudy weather", [amused] and today is cloudy. [short pause] [intrigued] The plan is a puzzle box: every principal room has two or more ways in and out, and the passages are "so planned that servants rarely are in evidence". [short pause] [softly] So while the needles go in and out in the library, a whole second household is moving round them unseen: the cook, the maids, the man who keeps the fires. Frances Glessner wanted a house where the work never showed. [chuckles] She got one. [short pause] The ladies sew... The reader reads. And the help keeps out of sight in the court, [whispers] where only you can see them.
scripts.stop:bench: [intrigued] The service stair, down to the basement. Down there is the newest room in the house: the workbench Frances Glessner set up this year, where she makes silver with a hammer and a torch and stamps each piece with "a G encircling a honeybee". [short pause] [amused] Upstairs she is the most correct hostess in Chicago. Downstairs she is a craftsman taking lessons from a Hull House jeweller. [short pause] Both are true, and she has been running this house, and that class, by the clock for eleven years. [long pause] [quietly] But across Eighteenth Street a neighbour has been ill for a long time, and this morning the doctor is calling again. [short pause] Look out through the gates toward the corner house: the house of William W. Kimball, the piano maker.
scripts.stop:kimball: [measured] 1801 Prairie, across Eighteenth Street: the Kimball house. William Wallace Kimball came to Chicago in 1857 and traded his Iowa land for four pianos, which he sold from a second-floor office. Now his factory turns out about a hundred pianos and organs a week, and his name is on pianos all over America. He and his wife Evaline have no children. [long pause] [softly] And he is dying. [short pause] He will die "at home after a lingering illness" on 16 December, and his funeral will be held in this house. [short pause] [quietly] Watch the doctor going up the steps, and the steward who lets him in. [short pause] Among his honorary pallbearers will be "Marshall Field, Robert T. Lincoln" and, from the house of the Reading Class, "J. J. Glessner".
scripts.ending:clock: [softly] End of the walk. W. W. Kimball died on 16 December 1904, and John Glessner crossed Eighteenth Street to stand among his honorary pallbearers. [short pause] [warmly] The Reading Class went on. It met every Monday from October to May, "until 1930". [short pause] [tenderly] When Frances Glessner died, her husband tried to say who she had been. "She had a clean and wholesome and orderly mind, a heart overflowing with love for family and friends and for all in any need." [long pause] [thoughtful] That is the house in one sentence: clean, wholesome, orderly, and full of people you never see.
